title: Too Close for Comfort
caption: The core of the globular cluster NGC 6397, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope

recognition.text: NASA Hubble image release (STScI). No published audience rating.

story: Stars crowd the core of NGC 6397, one of the nearest globular star clusters, 8,200 light-years away in the constellation Ara. A globular cluster is a dense ball of old stars, and here they are packed about a million times more tightly than in the Sun's neighborhood, only a few light-weeks apart.

In such a crush, collisions happen, though only every few million years or so, and near misses are more common. Two stars that merge can form a blue straggler, a hot, bright star, and several stand out near the center. Close passes can also pair a normal star with a white dwarf, which pulls gas off its partner. These cataclysmic variables change in brightness and shine strongly in ultraviolet and blue light, and a few show as faint blue or violet stars.

An unexpected result was three faint blue stars near the center, colored turquoise, that do not vary at all. They may be very-low-mass white dwarfs, left behind when giant stars lost their outer layers early, perhaps through a collision or a binary companion.

understand.summary: Hubble's Wide Field Planetary Camera 2 took the data, mostly through ultraviolet and blue filters with a few green and infrared images. The exact color mapping is not published.
understand.eye: The cataclysmic variables stand out in ultraviolet light that the eye cannot see, and 7 hours of exposure gather far more light than an eye can.

behind.technique: Not stated by the source (single frame, stack, mosaic or panorama unknown).

explore: To find the variables, astronomers took 55 images over about 20 hours, mostly through ultraviolet and blue filters, and compared every star's brightness across them. They also identified nearly 100 ordinary white dwarfs spread throughout the cluster, the brightest of which appear as faint blue stars. The mosaic combines archival data from 1997 and 1999 with Hubble Heritage observations from 2001.
